speechtext: The same as the last law.

subsubtopic: DIVORCE AND COROLLARY RELIEF ACT FAMILY ORDERS ENFORCEMENT ASSISTANCE ACT MEASURES TO ENACT
speechtext:
The last law is very unsatisfactory in that respect. We certainly heard of cases where the spouse has gone
May 22, 1985

to court claiming physical cruelty and was told that she wasn't beaten hard enough or there weren't enough bruises. The single beating or the beating she had was not enough.
It does not require a simple assault but one of a nature to render continued cohabitation intolerable. Judges have differed as to what they considered "intolerable". Therefore, people have been turned down on the grounds of physical cruelty because it was considered that a wife should be able to put up with some. It is a question of what is intolerable, and I question whether that wording is adequate for this day and age. There is also the issue of the one year separation and whether it is an adequate period to establish marriage breakdown.
I certainly have had representations in my riding, particularly from clergy, who believe that perhaps a longer period of separation might provide an opportunity for a marriage to be saved. That is a reasonable and important point to be made and it is difficult to choose a particular cut-off period. While I am not opposed to a one-year proposal, I would be glad to hear representations concerning a different period of time.
One can note that lawyers in such cases, as the courts themselves, have an obligation to work toward reconciliation and advise clients as to the possibility of marriage counselling. The court has an obligation to stop the proceedings if it believes there is a possibility for reconciliation. I believe that the legislation treats the obligation of seeking reconciliation and avoiding marriage breakdowns seriously.
With respect to the issue of enforcement machinery, there are enormous improvements in this legislation. However, one can question whether the legislation goes far enough. I might point out that the New Democratic Party opposed the previous legislation in principle simply on the grounds that it did not have adequate enforcement machinery. We worked very hard with women's organizations in the country to ensure that adequate machinery would be introduced. We fought for that very vigorously, and it is a great pleasure to see that these objections have been taken seriously.
However, organizations are saying that it is not good enough yet. Let me quote the Canadian Advisory Council on the Status of Women:
The proposed legislation only offers increased access to information on spouses who default on support and custody orders. It should provide enforcement of these orders.
The CACSW again calls for a national enforcement agency which would begin the enforcement process when a spouse defaults on payment and which would also have the authority to garnishee wages and other income sources. Without such an agency, people in need-and that is mostly women-will still have to initiate lengthy legal proceedings to get the payments they have already been awarded by the provincial courts.
This is a thorny legal question of jurisdiction between the federal and provincial Governments. I would like to see the provinces do more. Certainly, Manitoba is proving that automatic computer monitoring is successful is getting maintenance orders actually paid, and it would be beneficial for other provinces to follow suit.
The United States Government has been far more aggressive in encouraging the collection of maintenance payments. In
Divorce Acts
my Party, one seldom has the opportunity to congratulate President Reagan on anything. However, in this case, if not for the right reasons, we do see some action. The purpose for his action is to save welfare payments on the part of the state. Nevertheless, bless Ronald Reagan for ensuring that women get their maintenance payments. The federal Government in the United States accomplished this by paying 75 per cent of the enforcement costs. The Government could at least consider such a mechanism. Certainly, the provincial and federal Governments should consider the establishment of much greater enforcement machinery.
Let me refer to a study by Finnbogason and Townson which raises serious doubts about the proposal before us today. What it says is that such an agency, if it is only going to have information in it and not be linked into actual enforcement, may not be cost effective. Why set one up if it is only going to have those purposes? It points out that the experience of Manitoba and other jurisdictions, such as the United States, indicates that effective enforcement of maintenance orders is a matter of regular monitoring of accounts, prompt notification of default, and vigorous pursuit of defaulters. Such requirements are only met through an automatic computerized state initiated enforcement system. The establishment of such a system should therefore be a priority in each province where it does not already exist.
If all Canadian jurisdictions were to adopt such a system, then a central registry could become an effective part of a nationally linked system for monitoring and enforcement of maintenance and custody orders. However, to confine a central registry to the passive role of a mere repository for the purposes of providing information on maintenance and custody orders is to develop a very expensive computerized filing system which would do little to improve the day to day enforcement of maintenance and custody orders and to relieve the desperate financial situation of so many Canadian single parent families. These are strong words and I think they are very appropriate. I think this is an area where we still need to see more work done.
The legislation does provide adequate safeguards for the abuse of privacy. This has been a traditional objection, and I think these objections are quite properly answered in the legislation. It would remove the barriers to the garnishment of federal moneys, including income tax refunds, unemployment insurance, Canada Savings Bond interest, Canada pension plan payments, old age security, guaranteed income supplements, and this list could even be extended. The important point is that there is recognition of responsibility to pay for the support of children and the people looking after them, normally the mother. A person does not have the right to say this money is mine for my use alone, but a recognition that marriage is a partnership, that family involves responsibilities of both the parents. This is a most important reform, that the right of a person to income, and the responsibility to support other people in the family unit be recognized. It is a point I

May 22, 1985
Divorce Acts
have argued in the House on a number of occasions, and I am very glad to see it being recognized in the legislation today.
I have a couple of points on a few other matters in the legislation. With respect to variation orders, here we see some better recognition of the reality of Canadian mobility patterns. It is a reasonable compromise. This will allow for greater flexibility in varying orders for maintenance and also for custody. Also, there are some better safeguards than in the Liberal legislation of last year to prevent one's spouse from moving to another province just to get a variation order that the dependent spouse could not fight. The reform, which is a very sensible one, requires that the new order be confirmed in the court of the province where the concerned spouse actually lives so there cannot be this evasive action which we know occurs. This was a recommendation of the National Action Committee on the Status of Women of Canada. It shows Common sense has prevailed and that a good recommendation has been incorporated into the legislation.
There is a similar provision for custody where a child is in one province with one parent and the other parent applies for custody. The parent who has the child can apply to have the case heard in their province so that the information on the child's welfare can be brought to the court and the decision will not have to be made in a distant place where the other parent is. In other words, the needs of the child concerned will be treated seriously by the court. It will be possible to get the information on those needs to the court.
Finally, there will be greater flexibility in allowing the provinces to determine the nature of the court procedures for divorce. This will permit provinces, although it will not require them, to avoid trials on uncontested matters. This is a proper procedure, allowing these decisions to be made by the provinces. Some will probably choose to insist on having court appearances, and some will dispense with that procedure.
To conclude, Mr. Speaker, I have a great deal of satisfaction in seeing the many improvements in the legislation before us. I think it goes to show that democracy is indeed alive, that common sense can prevail, that Ministers of Justice can listen
to constituents, organizations, and what Opposition Parties are saying. The Bills before us today still need some work. The NDP will support passage of them. We want these Bills to go to committee for some modest amendments. They are a considerable improvement over previous legislation. It goes to show that an Opposition Party, by raising vigorous objections and making them in a very constructive way, can have a position impact in seeing real reform brought into legislation when a matter comes to Parliament.
